Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What do chefs typically do with leftover ingredients? Do they incorporate them into new dishes or throw them away?
Answer: When you see ‘chef’s surprise’ on a menu, you can bet it is a way to get rid of leftover ingredients. There is no time in a restaurant to get improvising as a well trained restaurant kitchen staff is trained to prepare dishes featuring on the menu, in the shortest time possible. Furthermore, it is not up to the chef to decide the quantity of ingredients to be purchased, that is work for the manager. Sometimes leftovers are given to the staff but usually they are, alas, binned. So one could conclude that ordering a ‘chef’s surprise’ is a noble act, saving ingredients from that somber destiny.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is your go-to appetizer at Italian restaurants and what do you enjoy about it?
Answer: When going to a restaurant that serves fish, a platter of of raw fish is hard to resist. Some Mazara prawn, a langoustine and some tuna tartare. Only trustworthy places offer raw fish, as it doesn’t come without risks. When the fish is not fresh, the joy is short-lived. Putting it on the menu is a sign of confidence and quality. You could argue serving raw fish is pretty easy, as you just peel the prawn or cut the the fish, and you’d be right. What really matters is that good restaurants have excellent fish suppliers offering stuff that we mortals have no access to.

Question: Is the type of water used to cook pasta important for its taste? If yes, what types of water are recommended for making pasta?
Answer: The type of water, as long as it is potable, doesn’t change the outcome of your pasta. The water is first of all brought to a boil, after which it is salted. Once pasta is boiled, it is added to a condiment or sauce.

Name: Ian De Pagie
Question: What is the standard serving size for spaghetti? Can this information be found online?
Answer: There is no such a thing as a universal standard serving. As there is no standard serving of sandwiches, potatoes or rice. In Italy people boil about one hundred grams per person (3.5oz). Where this satisfies Italians, there is a general tendency to increase that number.
